summary: Conflict between Armenia and Azerbaijan cut ordinary direct transport links in the early 1990s: a blockade affecting Armenia was established by summer 1991, while the blockade of Nakhchivan dates from June 1992. Responsibility for the latter was disputed. The interstate border was still reported closed in June 2025; subsequent rail shipments through Georgia did not establish a reopening of the direct border. Humanitarian routes and the Lachin corridor operated under separate arrangements.

verification.notes: Checked separate summer1991 Armenia and June1992 Nakhchivan blockades; through-Georgia rail is not direct frontier reopening.

summary: Türkiye withdrew limited transport access across its Armenian border in 1993, in response to Armenian advances in Azerbaijan, according to historical accounts. Ordinary direct land travel and trade remained unavailable, although specifically authorised aid convoys, diplomats and border officials crossed on occasion. A Turkish statement in May 2026 said preparations to open the border were continuing; arrangements for trade through third countries did not reopen it.

verification.notes: 1993 concerns withdrawal of limited transport, not first universal inaccessibility; authorised convoys and May2026 preparation retained.

summary: Abkhaz de facto authorities abolished the Shamgona–Tagiloni crossing on 15 April 2016, saying that concentrating controls at Enguri would be easier and more effective. Local residents lost this route across the administrative boundary, although other crossings remained available. Georgia’s Public Defender confirmed the closure in November 2017, and a report covering 2023–2024 again described the crossing as abolished.

verification.notes: April2016 named-post abolition and administrative consolidation supported; later reporting period not exact observation date.

summary: Abkhaz de facto authorities closed Khurcha–Nabakevi and Orsantia–Otobaia in early March 2017, citing security concerns. The closures disrupted residents’ journeys for school, healthcare, family visits and trade, while alternative crossings remained available. Reports differ over whether closure began on 4, 5 or 6 March. Both posts were listed as closed in November 2022, and EU monitors separately confirmed the continuing closure of Khurcha–Nabakevi to regular traffic in November 2023.

verification.notes: March4–6 disagreement retained; November2023 EUMM confirmation applies only to Khurcha–Nabakevi.

summary: Abkhaz de facto authorities restricted ordinary departures through Enguri on 10–11 January 2019, citing H1N1 influenza prevention. Return into Abkhazia remained possible under the initial rules, with additional exceptions for medical cases, hydroelectric-plant staff and visa-holders. Local accounts reported ordinary passage resuming on 5 February, although screening continued and authorities described the restoration as temporary and subject to reassessment.

verification.notes: Departure-specific H1N1 restriction, return/medical exceptions and February5 actual but conditional resumption match evidence.

summary: South Ossetian de facto authorities restricted ordinary passage across their controlled crossings on 11–12 January 2019, citing H1N1 influenza; Georgian authorities disputed that justification. A special humanitarian window allowed listed travellers to leave on 20–22 February, while entry remained restricted. Ordinary crossings resumed on 15 March, according to EU monitors and contemporary reporting.

verification.notes: January onset bounds, special February exit window and March15 ordinary reopening remain distinct; Georgian disagreement attributed.

summary: Abkhaz de facto authorities restricted ordinary travel through Enguri from 27 June 2019 following protests in Tbilisi and Zugdidi, which they described as a threat to Abkhaz statehood. The measure affected residents travelling between Gali and Georgian government-controlled territory. Children and older people received limited permission to cross from early July, and the formal restriction on other ordinary travellers was lifted on 2 October.

verification.notes: Enguri-only ordinary cohort excludes children/older travellers; October2 is formal lifting, not all-traffic observed reopening.

summary: Residents using the Rishtan–Sokh route between Uzbekistan and its exclave continued to face blocked access after a disputed reopening ceremony in August 2019. Kyrgyz officials cited phytosanitary and veterinary requirements, but accounts do not establish whether the route briefly reopened before closing again. Kaytpas and Otukchu were formally reopened for pedestrians and passenger vehicles on 1 April 2021; freight vehicles remained prohibited, and longer alternative routes had remained available.

verification.notes: Disputed August2019 operation not used as exact onset; April2021 passenger permission preserves freight exclusion and alternatives.

summary: South Ossetian de facto authorities closed Odzisi and Sinaguri on 4 September 2019 amid confrontation over a Georgian police post near Chorchana–Tsnelisi, disrupting local journeys including those of Akhalgori residents. Medical and holiday permissions allowed some exceptional crossings. Limited monthly access at Odzisi began in August 2022, and a Thursday–Sunday schedule was documented from early September 2026. These arrangements restored some access rather than unrestricted daily passage.

verification.notes: Verified original two-post closure, Odzisi-only monthly endpoint and later Thursday–Sunday schedule without precise September start.

summary: Azerbaijan introduced COVID-19 restrictions on passenger entry from Iran, Georgia and Russia in stages between late February and mid-March 2020. Ordinary foreign entry by road into mainland Azerbaijan remained restricted in September 2026, while freight and individually authorised entry were exempt and foreign nationals faced different exit rules. Passenger rail permission from Georgia resumed in May 2026, so the road restriction should not be read as a continuing ban on every form of land travel.

verification.notes: Staged frontier onsets and road-only mainland admission correctly distinguished from Georgia rail permission and foreign exit.

summary: Afghan authorities closed Islam Qala on the Iranian frontier on 23 February 2020 as coronavirus spread in Iran. The restriction affected passengers, particularly Afghans trying to return home. A local account reports reopening the following day after pressure from stranded returnees; it does not establish the same timetable for every crossing on the Iran–Afghanistan border or for freight.

verification.notes: Local Islam Qala returnee account supports next-day reopening without extending to all Iranian frontier freight.

summary: Armenia restricted passenger land transport with Iran in February 2020 to prevent COVID-19 transmission. The Iran-specific regulation took effect on 25 February, while allowing controlled freight movements, citizens returning to their own country and specified official or resident travellers. That regulation was repealed on 22 March, but overlapping national pandemic restrictions continued, so repeal did not itself mean that ordinary border travel resumed.

verification.notes: February25 effective date and March22 repeal correct; overlapping national rules mean no operational reopening claim.

summary: Abkhaz de facto authorities began restricting travel through Enguri on 27 February 2020 to prevent COVID-19 transmission, widening the closure in mid-March. Ordinary residents faced prolonged limits, but temporary return corridors and permissions for pensioners, medical cases and other specified groups allowed some crossings. Passage for people holding crossing permission was restored from 5 July 2021; this was not unrestricted access for everyone.

verification.notes: Initial foreign-tourist refusal and later broad Enguri regime correctly distinguished; permit-holder July2021 restoration preserves special corridors.

summary: Georgia restricted foreign passenger entry during the COVID-19 pandemic, first at several neighbouring frontiers and then generally from 18 March 2020. Georgian citizens, eligible family members, freight workers and other authorised travellers were exempt. Georgia permitted land entry again under health conditions from 1 June 2021, although this decision did not remove neighbouring countries’ restrictions or establish when every crossing first resumed carrying passengers.

verification.notes: General March18 phase is later than some frontier restrictions; June1 legal permission does not override partner-state rules.

summary: Kazakhstan introduced pandemic restrictions on entry and exit in March 2020, with exemptions for freight, returning citizens and other specified travellers that changed over time. Restrictions on foreign entry at land crossings with Russia, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan were eased on 11 April 2022, while health requirements remained. Kyrgyz nationals were reported crossing at Ak-Jol that day; the evidence does not establish equivalent reopening at the Chinese or Turkmen frontiers or one unchanged restriction throughout the pandemic.

verification.notes: Three named-frontier foreign-entry easing and observed Ak-Jol passage are scoped correctly; changing exemptions preclude uniform duration.

summary: Armenia restricted foreign entry under its COVID-19 emergency framework from March 2020, initially targeting travellers from or recently in designated high-risk countries. A September successor rule prohibited ordinary noncitizen land entry, with changing exemptions for residents, families, transport crews and other authorised groups. The land-entry prohibition was cancelled from 12 January 2021 with testing requirements retained; this was a changing set of rules rather than one unchanged ban on all foreigners.

verification.notes: High-risk-origin March restriction differs from September general noncitizen rule; January cancellation not transferred to citizen exit.

summary: Uzbekistan suspended ordinary international road passenger travel from 16 March 2020 to limit COVID-19 transmission, restricting foreign arrivals and Uzbek departures while allowing freight under special procedures. Uzbekistan announced general permission to resume road travel from 1 October, following earlier easing with Kyrgyzstan. Actual access also depended on neighbouring states’ rules, and individual frontiers reopened on different timetables.

verification.notes: March road prohibition and October national permission are supported, while earlier Kyrgyz and later bilateral access are separately qualified.

summary: Kyrgyzstan restricted entry by foreign citizens and stateless people from 19 March 2020 to prevent COVID-19 transmission. Citizens could return, foreigners could leave normally, and exemptions covered freight crews, diplomats, qualifying residents and family members, with further permissions added over time. The underlying order was repealed on 30 April 2022, ending an amended legal framework rather than proving that every traveller had been barred throughout.

verification.notes: Foreign/stateless entry only, normal departure and specific exemptions preserved; April2022 repeal is legal endpoint.

summary: Turkmenistan announced restrictions on foreign and stateless travellers entering from 20 March to 20 April 2020 to prevent COVID-19 transmission, with exceptions including diplomats, transport crews and specified business personnel. The announced expiry does not establish reopening. Tourists were documented entering by land in May 2023, and later travel guidance confirmed tourist access under invitation and guide requirements, but the first reopening date is not established.

verification.notes: Scheduled April2020 expiry not treated as reopening; May2023 tourist observation correctly distinguished from transit visas.

summary: Turkmenistan stopped ordinary through-transit by foreign road carriers in late March 2020 under its COVID-19 controls. Goods could still move through transloading, rail transport and later vehicle-handover arrangements, so the measure was not a complete cargo ban. Customs authorities reported that controlled transit on the Uzbekistan–Farap–Sarakhs–Iran route resumed from 1 June 2022, with sanitary requirements; sources differ by one day over the original start.

verification.notes: Foreign carrier transit, rather than all cargo, was restricted; reported June2022 route restoration and one-day onset conflict retained.

summary: Abkhaz de facto authorities restricted ordinary passenger entry through Psou from Russia on 28 March 2020 to prevent COVID-19 transmission. Specified diplomatic, military, business and freight movements were exempt. Travel by Russian and Abkhaz citizens was permitted again from 1 August, while restrictions on third-country nationals continued; this was distinct from the separate Enguri restrictions towards Georgian government-controlled territory.

verification.notes: Psou Russian/Abkhaz permission on August1 does not erase third-country limits or distinct Enguri regime.

summary: Uzbekistan restricted ordinary Afghan civilian entry through Termez–Hairatan during 2021, as COVID-19 measures overlapped with security concerns during the Taliban advance. Freight and specifically authorised movements continued, and later visits to a border free-trade zone did not amount to general admission. Passenger access for visa-holding citizens was reported restored from 23 November 2025. Sources place the initial suspension between June and August 2021, rather than establishing one precise start date.

verification.notes: Afghan civilian entry and June–August onset conflict correctly scoped; freight and free-trade-zone visits are not ordinary admission.

summary: Kyrgyzstan restricted the entry, exit and transit of Tajik nationals, vehicles and goods from 21 May 2021 following deadly border fighting and unresolved tensions. Diplomats, approved officials and people returning to their own country were exempt. Kairagach and Kyzyl-Bel formally reopened on 13 March 2025 after a border agreement, with thousands of passages reported over the following days; this evidence does not establish simultaneous restoration at every crossing.

verification.notes: Tajik nationality/goods restrictions and return-home exceptions supported; March2025 named-post permission not all-crossing restoration.

summary: Cargo movements through Aqina on Afghanistan’s Turkmen frontier were disrupted during the Taliban advance in mid-2021. On 4 July, a provincial official alleged that Taliban fighters had blocked the inland cargo road, while wider reporting also described fighting and port inactivity. Normal trailer and rail traffic at Aqina was reported in August, but that does not establish when the particular roadblock began or was removed.

verification.notes: Provincial Taliban-roadblock allegation attributed; August trailer/rail operation not represented as roadblock-clearance date.

summary: The Islam Qala–Dogharoun crossing between Afghanistan and Iran closed on 23 April 2022 after a confrontation over road construction near the border. Cargo movement resumed the following day, with a truck entering Afghanistan from Iran specifically documented. Passenger travel was reported operating by 26 April, but that later report does not establish that passengers had remained continuously barred until then.

verification.notes: Cargo reopening April24 and later April26 passenger evidence kept separate, without assuming passenger closure between them.

summary: Access along the Lachin corridor between Armenia and Nagorno-Karabakh was obstructed from 12 December 2022 by protesters advancing environmental demands, and Azerbaijan later tightened controls, citing security and illicit traffic. Ordinary civilian travel and essential supplies faced prolonged restrictions, while some Red Cross aid deliveries and medical evacuations continued. Aid passage was documented on 18 September 2023 and refugees crossed out to Armenia later that month; neither establishes unrestricted two-way reopening.

verification.notes: Environmental and security claims attributed; ICRC and outward-refugee access are not unrestricted two-way reopening.

summary: Abkhaz de facto authorities restricted departures through Enguri from 7 April 2023 ahead of an opposition rally in Tbilisi, citing safety and possible destabilisation. Entry into Abkhazia remained unchanged, while elderly people, medical travellers and hydropower staff could leave under exceptions. The restriction was formally lifted on 10 April; the available account does not separately time the first restored ordinary crossing.

verification.notes: Exit-only Enguri restriction preserves inbound access and exceptions; April10 lifting not website modification date.

summary: The Milak–Zaranj commercial crossing between Iran and Afghanistan closed after clashes between Iranian forces and the Taliban on 27 May 2023. An Iranian transport official reported that commercial exchanges resumed on 28 May. The clashes occurred amid tensions over Helmand water, but the evidence does not establish water disputes as the cause of the closure or confirm the same timetable for passenger traffic.

verification.notes: Named official supports commercial reopening May28; Helmand-water context is not claimed as established closure motive.

summary: South Ossetian de facto authorities announced that the Razdakhan and Pereu crossings would not operate during October 2024, citing elections and alleged provocations. This suspended access that was already limited to monthly opening windows. Reporting also describes a 25–28 October security-duty period as a closure interval, but the conflicting wording does not establish those as the precise closure and reopening dates or confirm actual resumption.

verification.notes: October nonoperation notice and enhanced-duty clock conflict accurately retained; no actual resumption inferred.

summary: Abkhaz de facto authorities restricted ordinary travel through Enguri from 23 October 2024 during the Georgian election period, citing the possibility of provocations. Returning residents and electricity-system personnel were exempt, so the measure did not stop every crossing in both directions. Local reporting confirmed people crossing both ways again on the morning of 30 October.

verification.notes: October23 commencement and October30 observed two-way traffic match sources, with returnee/electricity exceptions.

summary: Tajikistan restricted foreign and stateless travellers’ entry and exit during the COVID-19 pandemic, with exemptions for diplomats, international organisations and transport crews. Normal procedures at the Uzbekistan frontier were formally restored from 15 March 2022, subject to health documents. A traveller was reported driving from Tajikistan into Uzbekistan a week later, but the evidence does not establish the precise beginning of the matching restriction or simultaneous restoration of every type of journey.

verification.notes: March2022 legal restoration and later outward drive not confused with foreign inward access or exact2020 onset.

summary: Uzbekistan and Tajikistan restored operation at eight local road checkpoints from 1 March 2018 during a diplomatic rapprochement. Earlier restrictions, associated with border and political disagreements, had curtailed local travel and trade for years, while other routes such as Dousti and Fotehobod remained available. The announcement covered Jartepa, Kushkent, Uchkurgan, Khavastabad, Bekabad, Pap, Ravat and Gulbahor; their individual first closure dates are not established.

verification.notes: Eight road posts exactly match announcement; rail and still-open routes distinguished, individual historic onset unknown.

summary: Pakistan closed Afghan crossings on 16 February 2017 after militant attacks, alleging that attackers operated from Afghanistan; Afghan authorities denied sheltering them. Freight through Torkham resumed on 21 March, following a reopening order the previous day. Temporary return journeys by Afghans earlier in March did not restore trade, and some passenger restrictions continued after the general reopening.

verification.notes: Torkham freight endpoint is actual March21 trucks, not March20 order or earlier returnee passage; security allegation attributed.

summary: Pakistan closed the Chaman crossing after border clashes linked to a census operation on 5 May 2017. Commercial freight resumed on 27 May, when authorities reopened the crossing citing humanitarian considerations during Ramadan. Some Afghan passport and visa holders and urgent medical travellers had already been allowed through, so the freight interruption does not describe an equally long closure for every passenger.

verification.notes: Chaman freight restart May27 supported; earlier passport/medical permissions and reopening rationale remain separate.

summary: India suspended barter trade at Salamabad and Chakkan-da-Bagh across the Kashmir Line of Control from 19 April 2019. The government alleged that the trade was being used for weapons, drugs, illicit currency and militant-linked activity; those claims are its stated justification. Salamabad was still reported inactive in September 2026, when its premises were transferred for tourism use, but that later evidence does not establish the status of Chakkan-da-Bagh or passenger movement.

verification.notes: Official illicit-trade allegations retained as attribution; September2026 Salamabad observation not extended to other post or passengers.

summary: Pakistan suspended bilateral goods trade with India in August 2019 in response to India’s changes to Jammu and Kashmir’s constitutional status. Pharmaceutical products were exempted in September, while other trade remained suspended according to a February 2026 parliamentary statement. The restriction affected land commerce including Attari–Wagah, but it did not prohibit every passenger journey or apply identically to separate arrangements for Afghan transit goods.

verification.notes: August2019 original trade suspension correctly precedes September medicine exemption; 2026 parliamentary continuation and transit distinction checked.

summary: India and China suspended regulated local trade at their designated Himalayan passes during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. The Sherethang–Nathu La trading season was formally reopened on 1 August 2026, with trade resumption confirmed later, although the first consignment is not precisely dated. Developments at Lipulekh and Shipki La had their own timetables, so the Nathu La dates do not establish simultaneous operational reopening of all three routes.

verification.notes: Nathu La formal August2026 reopening separated from first consignments and other Himalayan passes.

summary: Pandemic restrictions prevented normal seasonal passenger travel through Khunjerab between Pakistan and China from resuming in 2020. Emergency permissions allowed some personnel and goods movements, and two-way cargo traffic resumed from April 2022. Ordinary passenger clearance was restored from 3 April 2023, with later reporting confirming passenger journeys; seasonal shutdowns and limited openings prevent treating the whole period as one uninterrupted closure to all traffic.

verification.notes: Missed2020 seasonal opening and emergency access not converted to universal closure; passenger April2023 permission distinct from2022 cargo.

summary: China stopped admitting Nepalese export goods through Rasuwagadhi on 29 January 2020 under its COVID-19 controls. Limited shipments from China into Nepal resumed earlier, leaving trade operating unevenly by direction. Nepal-to-China exports restarted on 27 December 2022, when the customs chief reported eight export containers crossing; a ceremony the following day did not mark the first restored exports.

verification.notes: Directional Nepalese export restriction, January2020 start and December27 actual containers supported; next-day ceremony excluded.

summary: Pakistan closed Chaman in early March 2020 to prevent COVID-19 transmission, then progressively allowed different kinds of movement. Food and essential-goods trucks entered Afghanistan on 21 March, while passengers remained subject to return windows and scheduled Saturday access. Broader passenger movement was confirmed restored by 21 August, so the earlier freight reopening and later passenger easing describe separate changes rather than a continuously sealed crossing.

verification.notes: Chaman freight and passenger phases correctly separated; August21 access bound agrees with supplemental status ledger.

summary: India suspended incoming passenger traffic through its immigration posts from 23 March 2020 as part of COVID-19 containment, including arrivals at land crossings. Goods vehicles and their crews remained exempt, and later rules allowed repatriation transport and authorised departures. An official notice confirmed continuation in May 2020; later visa changes and reopening of selected posts do not establish one common date when all affected land crossings resumed ordinary passenger admission.

verification.notes: March23 land subset of all-mode immigration rule verified; selected later reopenings do not supply common endpoint.

summary: Pakistan closed Torkham on 16 March 2020 to limit COVID-19 transmission, restricting passenger and trade movements. On 6 April, Afghan nationals with the required documents were allowed to return from Pakistan on foot during a temporary opening. That restored access for returnees did not reopen ordinary travel or vehicles generally, and later freight permissions followed separate schedules.

verification.notes: April6 endpoint limited to documented Afghan foot returnees, not ordinary travellers or vehicles.

summary: Bhutan restricted ordinary cross-border travel from 23 March 2020 to prevent COVID-19 transmission, while allowing returning Bhutanese subject to screening and quarantine. The national framework for approving Indian border-town workers’ daily journeys resumed from 23 September 2022. Implementation varied by crossing: dayworker approvals at Jomotshangkha were separately restored in July 2023, so the national date does not establish simultaneous reopening at every gate.

verification.notes: National dayworker approval framework and later Jomotshangkha implementation remain distinct; returning citizens excepted.

summary: Nepal announced passenger restrictions at its Indian and Chinese land borders from 23 March 2020, with extensions and exceptions for essential goods and authorised returnees. Restrictions on ordinary tourist travel lasted longer than the initial announced windows. Indian tourist vehicles were observed entering Nepal at Raxaul–Birgunj on 1 October 2021, but that reopening does not establish the same timing for all crossings or other categories of traveller.

verification.notes: Overlapping announced windows not added; observed October2021 endpoint limited to Indian tourist vehicles at Birgunj.

summary: Bangladesh tightened passenger admission from India on 26 April 2021 during India’s COVID-19 surge. Goods continued to cross, and approved Bangladeshi returnees could use designated ports subject to testing and quarantine. From 16 September, Bangladesh removed the special mission-authorisation requirement and restored regular hours at six operating ports; other ports and Indian-side arrangements followed separate timetables.

verification.notes: April26 entry tightening and September16 six-port NOC removal verified; cargo/returnees and later five ports not merged.

summary: Pakistan renewed restrictions on ordinary Afghan passenger admission through Torkham on 6 July 2021 because of rising COVID-19 cases. Cargo continued, and specified returnees, medical travellers, students and evacuees received permissions during the wider restriction. Admission for visa holders resumed on 21 October, with actual arrivals reported that day; separate brief Taliban interruptions did not constitute one additional continuous closure.

verification.notes: July6 renewed COVID tightening and October21 observed visa-holder entry match sources; freight and authorised cohorts retained.

summary: The Taliban closed Chaman on 6 August 2021 to press Pakistan to admit Afghans under less restrictive identity-document rules, disrupting both people and goods. Reports place restored pedestrian access between 11 and 13 August, including nationals returning home. The accounts differ over when reopening took effect, so they do not support one precise end date or the assumption that unrestricted visitor and freight traffic resumed on exactly the same schedule.

verification.notes: Taliban documentary-pressure action supported; conflicting August11–13 passage accounts and returning-national scope remain qualified.

summary: The Taliban briefly stopped pedestrian passage at Torkham on 13 September 2021 to press Pakistan over admission of Afghan citizens; stranded nationals could return home the following day, while trade had continued. A separate interruption on 23 September affected Pakistani pedestrians entering Afghanistan and produced a reported trade backlog before reopening later that day. These episodes did not lift Pakistan’s separate COVID-19 limits on ordinary Afghan entry.

verification.notes: Two discrete September pedestrian interruptions separated from continuing Pakistani COVID rule; first interruption did not stop trade.

summary: Chaman closed on 5 October 2021 during a dispute over the documents required for Afghans to enter Pakistan. Accounts differ over which side initiated the closure and how security and COVID-19 concerns contributed. Commercial trucks were reported crossing in both directions again on 2 November; an earlier brief opening for urgent medical patients had not restored freight traffic.

verification.notes: Competing imposing-side accounts preserved; November2 freight reopening distinguished from urgent medical window.

summary: Nepal ordered a temporary border seal for its 13 May 2022 local elections, allowing emergency and authorised passage. At Sonauli–Belahiya, ordinary Indian visitor vehicles and tourist buses were stopped from the night of 10–11 May, with traffic restored on 13–14 May according to differing reports. Nepalese returnees, ambulances and travel towards India were treated differently, so the documented vehicle restriction should not be read as a complete three-day halt to all movement.

verification.notes: Vehicle-specific observed restriction retains May10–11 and May13–14 bounds; national scheduled seal not universal observed halt.

summary: China suspended cargo movements into Nepal through Rasuwagadhi during a COVID-19 outbreak in Tibet in early August 2022. Contemporary reporting places the start on the weekend of 6–7 August. Seven inbound containers crossed on 15 September as authorities released stranded festival consignments; this limited resumption did not restore Nepalese exports into China or establish unrestricted two-way trade.

verification.notes: Contemporary August6–7 onset takes priority over later inconsistent August14 claim; September release limited to inbound festival cargo.

summary: China stopped cargo movements into Nepal through Tatopani on 10 August 2022 amid COVID-19 cases and restrictions in Tibet. Limited releases of stranded festival goods began on 10 September, when three trucks crossed, followed by five the next day. Officials described this as temporary clearance of a backlog, rather than an unrestricted reopening of the crossing to all trade or passengers.

verification.notes: August10 contemporaneous onset and September10 first three trucks verified; backlog release not general reopening.

summary: The Chaman Friendship Gate closed on 13 November 2022 after a Pakistani security guard was shot, amid disputed allegations about responsibility. Pedestrian and commercial traffic through the main gate resumed on 21 November. Some people had returned home through a separate emergency route during the closure, so the eight-day interruption concerns the main gate rather than every available route across the border.

verification.notes: Main Chaman gate closed after shooting; emergency-route returnees do not end named-gate interruption, responsibility remains disputed.

summary: Authorities in adjoining Nepalese and Indian districts announced three days of border restrictions from 18 November 2022 for Nepal’s parliamentary and provincial elections. At Belahiya, reporting on 19 November still described people crossing after checks, alongside permissions for patients and essential goods, while others waited. A fuller suspension was planned for polling day, but the evidence does not confirm an uninterrupted three-day closure or a precise operational reopening.

verification.notes: Announced three-day seal qualified by November19 checked passage; no unobserved polling-day or reopening converted to fact.

summary: The Taliban closed Torkham on 19 February 2023 during a dispute over medical travellers’ admission to Pakistan. Freight briefly crossed on 23 February before Pakistani authorities closed the crossing again; pedestrians were reported moving both ways the next day while trade remained suspended. Commercial traffic resumed on 25 February, so the disruption comprised two freight closures separated by a short opening.

verification.notes: Trucks crossing February23 then Pakistani reclosure require two spells; February24 pedestrians separated from February25 freight.

summary: Torkham closed to people and goods on 6 September 2023 after an exchange of fire during a dispute over construction near the Pakistan–Afghanistan border. The sides gave competing accounts of responsibility. Pedestrian passage and customs clearance for import, export and transit vehicles resumed on 15 September, following a nine-day interruption measured by the reported dates.

verification.notes: Construction-related gunfight and competing claims accurately attributed; September15 actual pedestrians and customs processing supported.

summary: Protesters obstructed truck movement at Chaman from 19–20 November 2023, opposing new passport and visa requirements that replaced local travel arrangements. Truck and highway restrictions were still documented in January 2024, and goods trade was reported restored by early March, although the first reopening date is unclear. The broader protest and disruptions to local passenger travel continued on different timetables, so their full duration cannot be treated as continuous freight closure.

verification.notes: Later March goods access agrees with status ledger; broad protest duration not used as continuous freight closure.

summary: Truck passage through Torkham stopped on 12–13 January 2024 during a dispute over Pakistan’s passport and visa requirements for Afghan drivers and reciprocal Taliban restrictions. Trucks resumed crossing on 23 January after an agreement, with a temporary grace period for drivers’ documents. This commercial reopening does not establish that all passenger categories were affected or restored on the same dates.

verification.notes: January12–13 source conflict and January23 actual truck movement retained, rather than prior agreement date.

summary: India suspended cross-border rail freight with Bangladesh from 19 July 2024, citing security concerns during student protests and political unrest. Freight on the Petrapole–Benapole rail link was still reported suspended in August, with resumed goods movements confirmed by early September, although accounts differ on the first reopening date. A separate road-trade interruption during the unrest remains excluded from the analysis because the evidence does not establish deliberate denial of passage.

verification.notes: Included rail and excluded road mechanisms correctly distinguished; by-September freight bound not applied to passenger trains.

summary: Torkham closed to people and goods on 21–22 February 2025 after a dispute over construction of a border post. Commercial trucks resumed crossing from both sides on 19 March. Ordinary documented pedestrian passage towards Afghanistan was reported restored on 22 March, while accounts disagreed over earlier patient access; the cargo reopening therefore does not establish that all passengers could cross at the same time.

verification.notes: February onset bounds and separate March19 cargo/March22 documented outbound passenger restoration preserved.

summary: India ordered Attari closed to ordinary passengers and goods on 24 April 2025 after the Pahalgam attack, citing alleged cross-border links. Exceptional Afghan cargo consignments entered in mid-May, and authorised returns and some pilgrim arrangements were handled separately. Ordinary tourist transit was still described as closed in 2026, so those exceptions and attendance at the border ceremony did not establish general reopening.

verification.notes: April24 MHA order distinguished from April26 circulation; exceptional Afghan trucks and pilgrim/ceremony activity are not tourist reopening.

summary: India barred Bangladeshi ready-made garments from land ports from 17 May 2025 and restricted other specified imports at selected crossings, later adding several flax and jute products. Designated seaport routes remained available, with exceptions for certain goods and transit to Nepal and Bhutan. The restrictions were still reported in October 2026; they controlled the routes for particular imports rather than closing the border to all goods or passengers.

verification.notes: Garment all-land-port ban and narrower other-goods routes retained; later jute additions and sea/transit exceptions supported.

summary: Pakistan–Afghanistan crossings closed after armed clashes in October 2025, with ordinary bilateral and transit trade through Torkham interrupted from 12 October. Afghan departures, returning empty Pakistani trucks and humanitarian aid were subsequently allowed under separate arrangements. Ordinary commercial traffic at Torkham was still reported suspended in October 2026; those exceptional movements did not amount to a general trade reopening.

verification.notes: Torkham commercial onset October12 distinguished from Chaman administrative date; departures, empty trucks and aid are exceptions.

summary: Authorities in Nepal’s Parsa district ordered ordinary border passage suspended from 3 to 6 March 2026 for the 5 March parliamentary election. Birgunj customs separately scheduled a shorter suspension of nonessential services, while fuel, medicines, food and some empty outbound freight vehicles received exceptions. Regular customs operations were reported resuming after polling, but that account does not establish the exact time ordinary passenger passage restarted.

verification.notes: Midnight-normalized March3–6 passenger schedule differs from March4–5 customs window; no passenger endpoint from customs resumption.

summary: Local routes around the Kyrgyz–Tajik border and Vorukh exclave were blocked from 13 March 2019 after a confrontation over road construction on disputed territory. The disruption affected residents and road users on the Isfara–Vorukh and Batken–Leilek corridors, with competing accounts of responsibility. The disputed section was reported reopened on 18 March after talks; this was a local access interruption rather than a closure of the entire frontier.

verification.notes: Local Vorukh and Batken access blockades, competing blame and reported March18 restoration supported; not whole frontier.

summary: South Ossetian de facto authorities ordered simplified crossings with Georgian-administered territory suspended from 8 to 11 June 2019 for election security. Reporting indicated closure on the first morning, but the later date came from the announced schedule. The evidence does not confirm when ordinary passage actually resumed or establish that every crossing listed in background accounts was normally operating before the order.

verification.notes: June8–11 security order is prospective; first-morning report does not establish June11 actual reopening or normally active five-post inventory.

summary: Traffic on the Isfara–Vorukh access road stopped on 22 July 2019 during violent clashes between communities near the Kyrgyz–Tajik border. The route reopened on 25 July, when injured people were reported being evacuated from Vorukh. Another affected corridor reopened at a different time, so these dates describe the exclave-access road rather than a uniform shutdown of the whole border.

verification.notes: Isfara–Vorukh July25 actual evacuation distinguishes endpoint from another road reopening July24.

summary: South Ossetian de facto authorities restricted passage through Ruk–Roki to Russia from 5 April 2020 to prevent COVID-19 transmission. Permissions evolved for returnees, official delegations, Russian servicemen, bereavement travel and authorised medical cases. Restrictions for Russian and South Ossetian citizens were formally lifted from 15 September, while third-country rules continued; the measure was separate from closures towards Georgian-administered territory.

verification.notes: Ruk/Roki link to Russia and September15 citizenship-specific lifting verified; Georgian-facing closures separate.

summary: Iran halted ordinary trade through Dogharoun and Mahiroud on 8 July 2021 as the Taliban advance created insecurity and Afghan officials left border facilities. Iranian exports in Afghan trucks resumed at Mahiroud on 10 July, initially slowly, while restoration at Dogharoun is documented between 10 and 15 July. Milak remained an alternative route, and these ordinary cargo movements differed from separate restrictions on international transit procedures.

verification.notes: Two July cargo endpoints correctly differ; Milak alternative and Afghan-carrier ordinary exports separate from TIR procedures.

summary: Uzbekistan restricted passage at Kara-Suu–Korasuv in February 2010, initially allowing people to return home before stopping passage in March. Officials cited low traffic or repairs, while observers offered political explanations that remained disputed. The crossing reopened on 12 September 2024 for Kyrgyz and Uzbek citizens travelling on foot during daylight; vehicles, animals and commercial freight remained prohibited apart from personal goods.

verification.notes: February return-only tightening and March full stop supported; September2024 pedestrian daylight reopening preserves cargo/vehicle exclusion.

summary: Nepal ordered Rasuwagadhi and Kimathanka closed to people and vehicles from 24 to 27 November 2017 for the first round of parliamentary and provincial elections. Freight was observed moving again through Rasuwagadhi on 27 November, with outbound containers and incoming trucks. That report confirms the return of cargo at Rasuwagadhi but does not independently establish when Kimathanka or every passenger category resumed operating.

verification.notes: Two-post announced election measure distinguished from Rasuwagadhi-only actual freight restoration.

summary: Nepal restricted India-facing crossings ahead of the 7 December 2017 parliamentary and provincial elections, citing security. Reporting on Kailali described restrictions from 5 December and an intended reopening on 7–8 December, but did not observe actual restoration. Conditions differed elsewhere: at Kakadbhitta, police said Nepalese citizens could enter with identification and travellers could leave for India, so the measure was not a uniform two-way ban.

verification.notes: Kailali planned endpoint remains unobserved; Kakadbhitta permissions not projected onto all crossings.

summary: Pakistan announced the closure of Chaman and Kharlachi on 24–25 July 2018 to secure its general election, while expressly keeping Torkham open for normal traffic. Reporting indicated that closure began, but other accounts gave a longer Chaman schedule and none established the first restored passage. The record therefore concerns two named crossings and an announced election measure, not a confirmed shutdown of the whole Afghan frontier.

verification.notes: Foreign Office named Chaman/Kharlachi and exempted Torkham; longer conflicting Chaman schedule acknowledged.

summary: Chaman closed after a clash over border fencing on 14 October 2018, interrupting commercial trucks, Afghan transit cargo and NATO supplies. Pedestrians resumed crossing on 15 October, while freight remained stopped until goods began moving both ways on 16 October. The longer interruption therefore concerns cargo, and accounts of which side initiated the confrontation remain disputed.

verification.notes: October15 pedestrians versus October16 freight distinguished; fencing-conflict responsibility unresolved.

summary: Pakistan closed Torkham and Chaman to ordinary pedestrian and cargo traffic from 19 October 2018 as a security measure for Afghanistan’s parliamentary election. Emergency cases were excepted, while travellers and trucks waited on both sides. People and freight were reported moving again on 21 October; this election closure followed a separate earlier clash-related interruption at Chaman.

verification.notes: Two-day election closure and October21 actual pedestrians/freight supported; emergency exceptions and separate earlier clash retained.

summary: Pakistan ordered its crossings with Afghanistan and Iran closed to pedestrians and cargo on 8 February 2024 for election security, with normal operations scheduled for the next day. Contemporary reporting confirmed closure at several Afghan crossings. The evidence does not establish the actual reopening time at each post, and a planned one-day shutdown does not demonstrate that the restriction lasted more than 24 hours.

verification.notes: All Afghan/Iran order distinguished from three observed Afghan posts; February9 resumption correctly remains scheduled.

summary: Uzbekistan stopped ordinary pedestrian service at Madaniyat during 2016, and limited crossing resumed on 1 October 2017 for nearby Kyrgyz and Uzbek residents during daytime hours. The exact closure date and reason are unclear: a separate motor-post suspension was attributed to repairs, but its relationship to the pedestrian restriction is unresolved. This entry remains excluded from the analysis pending clarification of whether it was a construction outage.

verification.notes: 2016 pedestrian restriction distinguished from separate repair-attributed motor suspension; exclusion remains explicit.

summary: Kyrgyzstan suspended Baymak–Kasansay under a May 2016 decree linked to Eurasian Economic Union customs and crossing requirements. Pedestrians and passenger cars resumed crossing on 19 September 2017 after permission and technical preparations, with daytime hours and baggage limits. Trucks remained barred, and the decree date does not establish the exact day the earlier suspension was first enforced.

verification.notes: Decree, effective and operational dates not conflated; September19 limited pedestrians/cars passage and EAEU attribution supported.

summary: Uzbekistan required Kyrgyz travellers using Dostuk–Dustlik to show documentation for qualifying family events, preventing ordinary visits without that justification. Passport-only crossings were reported on 6 September 2017 during improved bilateral relations, followed by a formal eligibility statement the next day. Accounts disagree about when the earlier conditions first began, and the evidence does not establish an unchanged restriction throughout the intervening years.

verification.notes: Conflicting original onset not resolved by retrospective claims; September6 actual passport passage precedes formal September7 statement.

summary: During the Taliban advance in July 2021, Afghan customs barred international transit cargo bound for Tajikistan under the TIR system from using Milak, because the onward Sher Khan crossing was closed. A 27 July transport bulletin described other traffic at Milak as permitted. The next bulletin used broader wording without explaining the change, so the precise start, any widening and the eventual lifting of this destination-specific restriction remain unclear.

verification.notes: Destination-specific Milak TIR ban correctly tied to onward Sher Khan closure; later broader bulletin not silently merged.

summary: Authorities stopped vehicles and freight at Sonauli on 26 June 2017 ahead of Nepal’s local elections, citing the need to prevent disruptive cross-border movement. Trucks queued on both sides, while pedestrians could cross after checks. The available report confirms the interruption that morning but does not establish when vehicles resumed; schedules reported for other Nepalese crossings cannot supply Sonauli’s reopening date.

verification.notes: Sonauli vehicles obstructed while checked pedestrians crossed; Biratnagar schedule not used as endpoint.

summary: Bhutan closed the Samdrup Jongkhar main gate on the evening of 14 September 2018 for its National Assembly primary election, stopping ordinary visitor entry and Bhutanese departures to India. It remained closed on 16 September, when reopening was expected later that day but not confirmed. Later reporting documents two-way access in September 2022; that supplies a later access date, not evidence of a continuous four-year closure.

verification.notes: Added supplemental September 2022 observed access without suggesting continuous 2018–2022 closure.

summary: Cargo operations at Tatopani–Zhangmu stopped in late January 2020 under COVID-19 controls, with accounts placing the start between 27 and 31 January. Medical supplies from China were first documented entering Nepal on 8 April after permission for limited essential imports. That shipment did not establish restoration of ordinary passengers, Nepalese exports or unrestricted two-way trade.

verification.notes: January27–31 cargo-onset conflict retained; April8 actual medical consignment not replaced by retrospective earlier date.

summary: China again suspended imports into Nepal through Tatopani on 6 October 2020 after workers tested positive for COVID-19, shortly after an earlier flood-related interruption had ended. A Chinese container entered Nepal on 29 October under restricted handling arrangements involving authorised workers and isolation areas. The resumption concerned imports into Nepal, not ordinary passenger travel or unrestricted two-way commerce.

verification.notes: October6 COVID reclosure separated from earlier flood outage; October29 actual inbound container supplies endpoint.

summary: Ordinary passport-holder passage at Benapole–Petrapole was suspended on 12 February 2026 for Bangladesh’s election, leaving passenger facilities largely deserted. Immigration services resumed on 13 February. Accounts conflict over whether emergency medical travellers were allowed through, and the scheduled 24-hour window does not establish that ordinary passenger restrictions actually lasted longer than a day.

verification.notes: Ordinary passport cohort excludes disputed medical exception; scheduled24hours not promoted to >24hours.

summary: Ordinary trade through Benapole–Petrapole stopped on the evening of 26 April 2026 under security arrangements for West Bengal’s election. Some medical passengers and limited perishable consignments continued to cross, and customs work inside the ports did not itself restore trade. Trucks resumed ordinary commercial movements on the morning of 30 April, according to port reporting.

verification.notes: April26 ordinary-trade halt and April30 trucks supported; internal customs/perishable exceptions distinguished.

summary: Uzbekistan restricted ordinary direct passage for residents of Kyrgyzstan’s Barak exclave through Ak-Tash–Birlishken from 16 January 2013 because the checkpoint lacked agreed authorisation. Emergency journeys and authorised supplies remained possible, while residents could use a longer alternative route. Direct resident passage resumed on 25 December 2018 after a bilateral agreement; the restriction did not mean that Barak had no access at all.

verification.notes: January16 contemporary onset and December25 resident passage verified; authorised emergency/supply and longer route retained.

summary: South Ossetian de facto authorities ordered simplified crossings with Georgian-administered territory closed from 7 to 10 April 2017 for presidential-election and referendum security. The measure affected permit-holding residents, including students, traders and people seeking healthcare, and reporting confirmed implementation on the first evening. The intended three-day window is documented, but actual reopening at its end is not confirmed.

verification.notes: First-evening implementation supported but April10 actual reopening unobserved; permit-holding local users correctly scoped.

summary: South Ossetian de facto authorities ordered simplified civilian crossings with Georgian-administered territory suspended around Russia’s presidential election in March 2018. The announced window ran from the evening of 17 March to the morning of 19 March, with security given as the reason. The notice did not separately identify freight treatment or exceptions, and the available evidence does not confirm actual reopening.

verification.notes: March17–19 scheduled civilian crossing restriction tied to Russian election, with freight scope unresolved.

summary: Ordinary cross-border passage in Nepal’s Parsa district, including Birgunj–Raxaul, was restricted from the night of 10 May 2019 ahead of voting in neighbouring Bihar. Officials cited election security and prevention of criminal activity, while petroleum tankers supplying Nepal remained exempt. Reports described differing two- and three-day schedules, but none established the exact time passage actually resumed.

verification.notes: Observed May10night commencement and conflicting planned lengths retained; petroleum exception applies to Nepal-bound supply.

summary: Authorities closed the Jhulaghat bridge between India and Nepal from 3 October 2019 for local elections on the Indian side. Ordinary users could not cross, although the two administrations could authorise emergency passage. Notices differed over whether restrictions would end on 5 or 6 October; later reporting confirms a multi-day closure but not the precise first restored crossing.

verification.notes: October3 Jhulaghat seal and differing October5/6 schedules preserved; emergency access and later retrospective duration qualified.

summary: Nepalese authorities announced that Jhulaghat would close from 22 to 25 November 2019 for legislative-election security on the Indian side. The restriction concerned ordinary users of the bridge, with emergency passage possible by agreement between the two administrations. The published dates describe the planned measure; the available evidence does not confirm its full implementation or the actual reopening.

verification.notes: November22–25 announced election window, not observed complete operation; mutual emergency permission retained.

summary: Bhutan announced the closure of its southern international gates from the evening of 29 November to the evening of 30 November 2023 for the National Assembly primary election. Polling-eve reporting confirmed that the gates had closed. The planned window was 24 hours, but the evidence does not establish the actual reopening time, detailed freight arrangements or exceptions at each gate.

verification.notes: Confirmed southern-gate election order and polling-eve implementation; retained scheduled 24-hour window without claiming observed reopening.

summary: India’s Tamulpur district restricted non-exempt people and vehicles using Bhutan-facing routes from the evening of 6 April 2026, citing election security and prevention of unlawful influence. Medical cases, specified documented travellers, checked essential perishables and eligible local voters received exceptions. The restrictions were scheduled to end with polling on 9 April, but their actual lifting is not documented.

verification.notes: Changed April 9 from an apparent observed endpoint to the scheduled end; preserved documented exceptions and election rationale.

summary: Bhutan announced entry and exit restrictions at Lhamoizingkha, Phuentsholing and Samtse from 20 to 23 April 2026 ahead of West Bengal’s first-phase election. Reporting confirmed closure at the Jaigaon–Phuentsholing route while allowing tourists and essential services. Those exceptions and implementation details are not established for all three gates, and the announced end does not independently confirm when ordinary passage resumed.

verification.notes: Checked all three named gates against the notice; confined observed implementation and exceptions to Jaigaon–Phuentsholing.

summary: Authorities in Nepal’s Banke district stopped residents making nonessential shopping trips through Jamunaha to the Indian market at Rupaidiha during the 2021 COVID-19 wave. Reports in March and April described restrictions, while essential work and screened returns into Nepal remained possible. Residents were documented shopping across the border again by July, but the first easing date and uninterrupted duration of the earlier limits are unclear.

verification.notes: Verified the restriction was in 2021, concerned outbound shopping, and later July shopping supplies access without an exact reopening day.

summary: Kyrgyzstan restricted non-exempt travellers at Irkeshtam and Torugart under a February 2020 order intended to prevent COVID-19 transmission from China. Returning citizens, diplomats and specified freight personnel were exempt, and cargo later followed separate health controls. The restriction was documented in May; an August 2023 Border Service announcement allowed pedestrians and car passengers at both gates on weekdays, with weekends freight-only. That later access does not establish the first passenger reopening date.

verification.notes: Added the supplemental August 2023 weekday passenger-access announcement for both gates, preserving exemptions and the unknown first restoration.

summary: Turkmenistan suspended rail freight through Sarakhs on the Iranian border in early April 2020 because of COVID-19, with sources differing between 1 and 2 April. Cargo wagons were reported moving in both directions again on 18 June, after weeks of suspension. An earlier statement that reopening preparations were complete did not itself establish restored traffic, and these dates concern rail rather than the road crossing.

verification.notes: Confirmed the April 1–2 source disagreement and actual June 18 wagon traffic; kept rail separate from roads.

summary: China renewed the freight suspension at Kulma–Karasu on the Tajik frontier in October 2020 under its COVID-19 controls. Goods handling resumed during April 2021, although the first day is not precisely established. Cargo was transferred between national vehicles, so this did not mean Tajik trucks or passengers could enter China; later reports distinguish direct truck admission from the earlier restoration of goods movements.

verification.notes: Checked October month-level onset and April goods restoration; preserved transloading versus direct Tajik truck and passenger admission.

summary: Milak–Zaranj closed on 5–6 August 2021 as insecurity intensified during the Taliban advance in Afghanistan. Passenger passage was reported restored on 10 August, followed by goods transit on 15 August. An intervening permission for already-stranded trucks was narrower than restoration of new commercial consignments, while Dogharoun and Mahiroud continued trading under separate arrangements.

verification.notes: Confirmed August 5–6 onset uncertainty, August 10 passengers and August 15 new goods movements; excluded other Iranian gates.

summary: India suspended travel and registration for the Kartarpur pilgrimage corridor from 16 March 2020 to prevent COVID-19 transmission. India-origin pilgrim journeys resumed on 17 November 2021, when a group was observed crossing to the shrine in Pakistan and returning. Pakistan’s earlier unilateral permission did not end India’s suspension, and other pilgrimage routes or domestic access to the shrine were separate matters.

verification.notes: Matched Indian suspension and actual November 17 pilgrim crossing; Pakistan’s earlier unilateral opening correctly remains separate.

summary: Vehicle traffic at Kharlachi on the Pakistan–Afghanistan border stopped on 21 September 2024 during tribal fighting in Kurram over land and defensive positions. Stranded vehicles crossed in both directions when the post reopened on 1 October following a ceasefire. Some reports gave inconsistent dates or rounded durations; the supported chronology concerns this crossing, not a closure of the entire Afghan frontier.

verification.notes: Checked September 21 against contradictory APP dating and confirmed October 1 vehicles both ways after the ceasefire.

summary: Rishtan–Kaytpas, a Kyrgyz–Uzbek crossing affected by restrictions after the 2013 Charbak conflict, briefly reopened and then closed again in September 2017. Citizen passage was reported restored from 25 September during daytime hours. The separate Apkan gate remained closed, preventing full access along the route to Sokh, and the evidence does not establish an uninterrupted closure from 2013 or equivalent access for freight and third-country travellers.

verification.notes: Confirmed the intervening September opening, September 25 citizen restoration, and continuing Apkan obstruction without inferring continuous closure.

summary: Freight workers interrupted India-to-Bangladesh traffic through Petrapole–Benapole on 24–25 January 2018 during a dispute over customs control of vehicle passes and processing delays. The stoppage later affected the opposite direction, while loading and unloading inside the port continued. Trade returned in stages on 29–30 January; those dates do not establish an identical interruption in both directions or a passenger closure.

verification.notes: Retained bounded onset and staged restoration; direction-specific refusal and continuing internal handling are supported.

summary: Traders stopped commercial freight at Petrapole–Benapole on 26 June 2018, demanding compensation for fire-damaged trucks, faster unloading and better facilities for drivers. The strike was withdrawn that evening, but actual truck movements resumed on 27 June. Passenger restrictions are not established, and the differing reported clocks do not show that the freight stoppage lasted more than 24 hours.

verification.notes: Checked trader demands, June 26 strike withdrawal and June 27 actual trucks; duration and passenger claims remain appropriately limited.

summary: Truck drivers blocked incoming goods from India at Hili in July 2018, demanding that rice be unloaded from vehicles stranded inside Bangladesh. A first action was lifted, and ten trucks entered on 3 July before the blockade resumed. Incoming cargo began crossing again on 5 July after unloading and negotiations; the documented interruption concerns that renewed blockade, not a continuous closure from 2 July or a passenger ban.

verification.notes: Verified ten arrivals preceded the renewed July 3 blockade and actual July 5 goods admission ended it.

summary: Freight movement through Petrapole–Benapole stopped on 8 January 2018 during a protest by customs-clearing representatives over alleged harassment, higher charges and processing problems. Trucks waited on both sides, while passport holders and internal cargo handling continued. Trade was operating again by 30 January after a separate later strike, but that observation does not establish when the 8 January stoppage ended or imply a continuous interruption.

verification.notes: Added January 30 as later restored-trade evidence while preserving the unknown end of January 8 and the distinct intervening strike.

summary: Iran stopped admitting tourist-visa holders from Afghanistan through Islam Qala and Zaranj in late December 2021, citing COVID-19 prevention. Business-visa holders were treated differently, so this was not a general passenger or freight closure. Later UN reporting places the end on 10 January 2022, but does not identify the first admitted tourist or establish exact operating hours; Islam Qala’s onset is reported as 24–25 December.

verification.notes: Matched tourist-visa scope, business exception, Islam Qala onset range and UNHCR terminal date without inventing first admission.

summary: Passenger travel into Iran through Abresham–Zaranj was disrupted in July 2022 amid tensions between Taliban and Iranian border forces. Documented travellers received temporary access on 6 July before further interruption, and an Afghan official reported legal passenger travel restored on 18 July. The earlier opening and uncertain reclosure date mean that the episode cannot be described as an uninterrupted two-week passenger shutdown.

verification.notes: Checked July 6 temporary documented passage and July 18 inbound legal passenger restoration; retained uncertain intervening reclosure.

summary: South Ossetian de facto authorities ordered civilian crossings with Georgian-administered territory suspended from the evening of 24 May to the morning of 26 May 2019. The security service said the measure was intended to protect school celebrations. The announced 34-hour window is documented, but the evidence does not establish individual crossing refusals, exceptions or when ordinary passage actually resumed.

verification.notes: Verified security-service election-free school-celebration rationale and 34-hour ordered window, with actual implementation unobserved.

summary: Authorities announced restrictions on ordinary passage along the Darchula–Dharchula frontier from the evening of 14 October 2019 for Indian local-election security. Emergency crossings could be authorised, and reporting indicated that sealing had begun. Notices differed over whether the measure would end on 16 or 17 October, leaving the actual reopening time and complete implementation at individual bridges unresolved.

verification.notes: Preserved conflicting October 16–17 planned endpoints, emergency discretion and reported October 14 sealing.

summary: Afghan returnee vehicles were refused passage at Torkham on 19 October 2026 during a reported checkpoint dispute. The interruption affected families travelling from Pakistan to Afghanistan with their belongings. Repatriation processing resumed after about two hours, making this a brief same-day episode; it did not establish that the separate restrictions on ordinary commercial trade had ended.

verification.notes: Checked the complete claims and phase: returnee-only refusal, reported checkpoint dispute and approximately two-hour resumption are supported.

summary: China stopped admitting organised Indian Kailash–Manasarovar pilgrimage groups through Nathu La in June 2017, citing security concerns linked to the Doklam confrontation. Pilgrims reported waiting at the closed gate, and the season was subsequently cancelled while the Lipulekh route continued. The first reported group in the following season crossed on 20 June 2018; this does not describe a year-long continuous closure to all traffic.

verification.notes: Confirmed organised-pilgrim scope, China’s attributed security rationale, season cancellation and actual June 20 2018 batch crossing.

summary: Traditional Nepal–China crossings used by local residents and traders were restricted during the COVID-19 pandemic from 2020. Nepal announced immediate restoration at seven points in May 2024, with others to follow, rather than simultaneous reopening of all fourteen mentioned in headlines. At Tiptala, thirty Nepalese traders were documented entering China on 24 May; exact closure and restoration dates differ by crossing and remain incomplete.

verification.notes: Checked seven immediately restored points versus fourteen headline points and separate May 24 Tiptala trader passage.

summary: Indian Kailash–Mansarovar pilgrims were barred from entering China through Hilsa after the route’s pandemic closure in March 2020. Earlier permission for local users or other travellers did not restore this pilgrimage route. Completed Indian pilgrim visits were documented by July 2025, but the first crossing date is unclear; seasonal inactivity also prevents treating the entire five-year period as continuous daily closure.

verification.notes: Matched March 2020 month-level onset and completed Indian pilgrimage visits by July 2025; seasonal and cohort distinctions are retained.

summary: Freight workers stopped imports and exports through Benapole–Petrapole on 12 October 2023 to demand the return of a deceased driver’s body. Trade resumed later the same day after assurances. Reports differ over the precise clocks, describing roughly eight or nine hours of disruption; the evidence concerns trucks and does not establish that passenger crossing was suspended.

verification.notes: Verified freight-only protest and same-day restoration; conflicting eight- and nine-hour clocks remain bounded.

summary: Pandemic restrictions interrupted the limited local access normally available through Korala on the Nepal–China border. Residents of Lo Manthang and Lo-Ghekar Damodar Kunda were documented visiting China again with border-area passes on 13–14 November 2023. This restored a restricted local travel arrangement, not unrestricted tourism or freight, and the original closure date is unclear because accounts differ and pre-pandemic access was already seasonal.

verification.notes: Checked local-pass eligibility and November 13–14 visits; differing pandemic onset accounts and pre-existing seasonal use remain explicit.

summary: Visitor access to the Khorgos cross-border shopping and tourism centre was suspended during the initial COVID-19 outbreak, following an earlier January 2020 holiday shutdown. More than one hundred Kazakh visitors were documented entering the Chinese section on 17 April 2023. The centre is separate from ordinary road and rail freight crossings, and its later formal reopening announcement did not mark the first restored visitor passage.

verification.notes: Verified January holiday/COVID distinction and April 17 visitor admission before the later reopening announcement; freight gates remain separate.

summary: Workers stopped freight exchange at Petrapole–Benapole on 21 December 2020 over staff access, handling delays and alleged harassment by Indian border personnel. Passport-holder movement and internal port work continued. Imports and exports resumed the next morning, according to port reporting; conflicting accounts of the strike’s starting time prevent establishing whether the stoppage lasted more than 24 hours.

verification.notes: Confirmed next-morning import-export restoration, continuing passengers/internal work and unresolved starting clock.

summary: Port users interrupted freight movement at Petrapole–Benapole on 30–31 January 2021, pressing demands over staff access, cargo handling and protection against layoffs. Most reporting described passport-holder passage as continuing. Goods traffic resumed on 2 February after trucks had been unable to cross for two days, while differing publication and update times leave the precise starting date uncertain.

verification.notes: Preserved January 30–31 publication ambiguity and February 2 actual goods passage; passenger treatment is cautiously attributed.

summary: Port users stopped cross-border freight at Petrapole–Benapole from 31 January 2022 over access and documentation rules and alleged harassment by management. Loading and goods delivery inside the port continued. Trucks were reported moving in both directions again on 5 February, after the strike had been withdrawn and a holiday intervened; the interruption to freight service was longer than the active strike itself.

verification.notes: Confirmed January 31 freight stoppage and February 5 bilateral truck counts; withdrawal, holiday and service restoration are distinguished.

summary: Truck associations halted goods exchange at Petrapole–Benapole on 30 July 2019, protesting alleged demands for unofficial payments and harassment. Travellers and internal port activities were reported unaffected. Bilateral freight resumed during the afternoon of 31 July, according to customs reporting, after a stoppage lasting longer than a day; accounts differ slightly over the reopening time.

verification.notes: Checked attributed payment allegations, unaffected travellers and July 31 afternoon actual freight return, with clock disagreement retained.

summary: Exporters stopped imports and exports through Hili on 30 August 2026, seeking permission to trade more commodities and improvements to port facilities. Passport holders continued to cross through immigration. Goods movements resumed on 5 September, although accounts differ over the time of day; the interruption concerned freight interchange rather than a general closure to people.

verification.notes: Matched August 30 exporter action and September 5 goods passage; passport-holder exemption and commodity/facilities demands are supported.

summary: Bangladeshi revenue staff protests over employment and institutional reforms stopped freight operations at Sonamasjid–Mahadipur and Benapole–Petrapole on 28–29 June 2025. Goods movements resumed on 30 June, with actual trucks reported at both ports. Earlier partial stoppages and later backlog clearance were separate from this complete freight interruption, and the evidence does not establish a matching passenger closure.

verification.notes: Verified Saturday/Sunday full stoppages and actual Monday trucks at both ports, without extending to earlier partial action or passenger movement.

summary: Kaplanbek–Navoi closed for reconstruction by early December 2022, interrupting ordinary passage between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. Limited personal travel was restored in late January 2025: official permission began on 27 January, and first passengers were reported by 29 January. Pedestrian, car and bus access remained subject to limits, while freight restoration was separate; a planned full-capacity opening did not prove that all traffic had resumed.

verification.notes: Verified closure already in effect by December 6 and bounded January 27–29 passenger return; freight and planned capacity remain distinct.

summary: The Zhibek Zholy–Gishtkuprik road crossing between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan closed to pedestrians and vehicles from 5 February 2025 for reconstruction and modernisation. Reports in October 2026 still described the two sides coordinating a reopening date. Completion of work on one side did not establish restored passage through the paired crossing, while alternative road routes and rail services remained separate.

verification.notes: Confirmed February 5 reconstruction closure and October 23 2026 pending paired reopening, without substituting one-sided construction completion.

summary: Passenger passage at Tazhen–Daut Ata between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan was suspended from 1 February 2025 for reconstruction safety. People, cars and buses were affected, while heavy freight continued. The passenger restriction was still reported in December despite technical commissioning on the Kazakh side; the evidence does not establish a paired reopening or justify extending the same restriction automatically through later undated reports.

verification.notes: Matched official passenger cohorts and continuing heavy freight through the dated December 29 report; undated later text does not extend status.

summary: Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan suspended ordinary passenger use of Atameken–Gulistan and Kazygurt–S. Nazhimov from 15 February 2023 during reconstruction, while heavy freight remained permitted. Personal passage at the Atameken pair was reported restored by March 2026, but its exact first reopening date is uncertain. Kazygurt passenger restrictions were still documented in November 2025; commissioning works on one side did not by itself establish that the paired route had reopened.

verification.notes: Checked both February 15 passenger measures, March 2026 Atameken access and unresolved Kazygurt return; commissioning and freight remain separate.

summary: Ken-Sai–Uch-Kurgan on the Kyrgyz–Uzbek border reopened on 12 September 2024 as a multilateral road crossing for people, vehicles, goods and animals. Reports described a longstanding interruption, but accounts of some earlier journeys conflict with claims that it had been continuously closed since 2009. The original official reason and exact periods of nonoperation remain unresolved, and the more restrictive rules at nearby Kara-Suu do not apply to this post.

verification.notes: Verified September 12 actual multilateral reopening and preserved conflicts over intervening historic journeys and unknown original motive.

summary: Pakistan restricted Ghulam Khan during the anti-militant military operation that began in North Waziristan in June 2014. Loaded commercial vehicles were documented entering Afghanistan again on 9 March 2018, before later trial and formal trade-opening announcements. That observed return concerns freight from Pakistan into Afghanistan, not restoration of all passengers or identical operating schedules in both directions.

verification.notes: Confirmed June 2014 onset precision and actual March 9 loaded vehicles into Afghanistan before later formal milestones.

summary: Pakistan closed Kharlachi to bilateral goods trade on 15 March 2020 as part of COVID-19 containment. The crossing was reported actually unsealed for commercial traffic on 11 July, after other Pakistan–Afghanistan crossings had reopened earlier. Those other posts’ timetables do not determine Kharlachi’s dates, and the available account does not establish when passenger travel resumed.

verification.notes: Checked Kharlachi-specific March 15 COVID restriction and July 11 commercial reopening without transferring other posts or passenger dates.

summary: Commercial traffic through Chaman was interrupted during fighting around Spin Boldak in July 2021. More than one hundred loaded trucks entered Afghanistan on 26 July when freight movement resumed. An earlier short opening for stranded nationals had not restored trade, and accounts do not give a consistent precise start date or an independently stated official reason for the original commercial restriction.

verification.notes: Confirmed actual July 26 commercial trucks, distinct July 25 stranded-national access and unresolved original onset and official rationale.

summary: Traffic through Chaman–Spin Boldak was interrupted during a clash on 11 December 2022. Accounts differ over restoration: one describes passage returning after a few hours that Sunday, another reports reopening on Monday, and a later account describes normal operations by Tuesday. Because they do not consistently distinguish passenger and freight movements, the evidence does not establish one continuous two-day closure or a precise first reopening.

verification.notes: Preserved Reuters/AP reopening disagreement and uncertain passenger/freight sequence; no continuous two-day closure is asserted.

summary: Pakistan restricted ordinary movement through Chaman from 27 September 2019 for security during Afghanistan’s presidential election. The measure affected people, vehicles and goods, with emergency patients excepted. Crossings were reported reopened on 29 September after the two-day election closure, although the accounts do not provide precise clocks for the first refusal and restored passage.

verification.notes: Matched September 27–29 election closure, government-attributed security and emergency-patient exception without inventing exact clocks.

summary: Commercial access at Angoor Adda was repeatedly reported restricted in 2024 amid disputes over travel documents and demands to reopen the crossing.
